newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan asks China for details on hijacker's return.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan asks China for details on hijacker's return.

text.p: Taiwan on Thursday asked arch-rival China to provide further details on Beijing's plan to repatriate a Taiwanese who hijacked a domestic airliner from the island to the communist mainland in March.

In a letter to Beijing's Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Strait, Taipei's semi-official Straits Exchange Foundation said it was pleased to learn of the China's plan but would like to know exactly when the man would be returned.

"Please inform us of the exact time and location for the transfer of the hijacking suspect Liu Shan-chung, relevant evidence, and police record, which can help our two sides to attack crime," the foundation said.
The Chinese Red Cross in the southeastern Chinese province of Fujian on Wednesday informed its Taiwan counterpart that Liu Shan-chung would be sent back to Taiwan by sea on May 14.
It asked Taiwan to quickly reply to the arrangement before May 7.
Beijing and Taipei have been rivals since the Communists won the Chinese civil war and drove the defeated Nationalists into exile on Taiwan in 1949.
The foundation, a front body charged with dealing with China in the absence of normal relations, said Liu would be tried under Taiwan anti-air piracy law.

Liu commandeered a Taiwan domestic airliner to Xiamen in southern China on March 10, becoming the first hijacker to force a passenger jet from the island to the mainland in the 1990s rather than the other way around.
In its letter, a copy of which was released to the media, the foundation said: "We are pleased to learn that our previous talks had borne fruit in resolving a case like this."
The foundation was referring to a series of talks between the sides in 1994 and 1995 on repatriation of Chinese hijackers, but those talks were bogged down by political and ideological differences.
Shortly after Liu forced the jet to Xiamen, Taiwan called on Beijing to return him and offered in exchange to repatriate two mainland hijackers who had completed their prison terms.
Taipei is holding 16 mainlanders who hijacked a dozen Chinese commercial airliners to Taiwan in the 1990s and were convicted of air piracy.
